The Rufous hare wallaby (Lagorchestes hirsutus) is a small macropodid marsupial endemic to arid and semi-arid regions of Australia. Females give birth to a single altricial joey weighing just 0.6 grams [Wwb = 0.6 grams] after a relatively brief gestation period of 30 days [tg = 30 days], a value derived from captive colony records maintained at a body temperature of 36.5 °C [T = 36.5 °C]. This gestation length is comparable to that of other small macropodids but notably shorter than in larger congeners, reflecting the accelerated reproductive schedule typical of desert-adapted marsupials. The neonatal mass is exceptionally low relative to the mother's size, as is characteristic of marsupials, and the underdeveloped neonate must complete its development within the maternal pouch. The mother's physiological state during this early lactation phase demands substantial energy, as the rapidly growing joey relies entirely on milk for its initial months of life. The timing of subsequent developmental milestones appears closely tied to the species' thermoregulatory costs in harsh desert conditions.

Juveniles typically attain nutritional independence from the mother at around 150 days after birth [tx = around 150 days after birth], a milestone measured under captive conditions at 36.5 °C [T = 36.5 °C]. At weaning, the joey reaches a body mass of approximately 500 grams [Wwx = approximately 500 grams], as documented by J. Courtenay in personal communications. This represents a roughly eight-hundred-fold increase from the birth mass, illustrating the remarkably rapid growth phase facilitated by the lipid-rich milk of the species. The weaning weight is an important ecological threshold, as it marks the point at which the young wallaby must begin foraging independently in a resource-poor environment. Following weaning, the juvenile enters a prolonged sub-adult period during which it continues to grow and accumulate body reserves while avoiding predation. This extended developmental phase is considered adaptive for a species inhabiting unpredictable arid habitats, where the timing of food availability varies considerably between seasons.

Sexual maturation in Lagorchestes hirsutus occurs at approximately 330 days since birth [tp = approximately 330 days since birth] when individuals are maintained at a typical body temperature of 36.5 °C [T = 36.5 °C]. By this age, the young wallaby has attained a wet body mass of roughly 1300 grams [Wwp = roughly 1300 grams], which coincides closely with the ultimate adult mass of the species. This pattern, where the mass at puberty nearly equals the maximum adult mass, is unusual among macropodids and suggests that these animals delay reproductive activation until they have nearly completed somatic growth. The close correspondence between pubertal mass and ultimate mass likely reflects selective pressures in an environment where early reproduction at a smaller body size would compromise survival during drought periods. Field studies indicate that wild individuals may not reach this mass threshold until later in their second year, particularly in years of low rainfall. The energetic demands of first oestrus and subsequent gestation require substantial body condition, which is often difficult to achieve in the unpredictable interior of Australia.

Fully grown adults of the Rufous hare wallaby achieve a maximum body mass of 1310 grams [Wwi = 1310 grams], representing the ultimate wet weight attained under favorable nutritional conditions. At this size, individuals are among the smallest members of the genus Lagorchestes, a body plan that facilitates concealment in spinifex tussocks. Records indicate that the average yearly milk production for a lactating female reaches approximately 21798.4 joules per day  when measured at a core temperature of 36.5 °C [T = 36.5 °C]. This daily energetic investment in lactation represents a significant proportion of the female's overall energy budget, a constraint that likely limits the maximum reproductive rate and contributes to the relatively small litter size. The milk composition of this species has not been studied in detail, but it is presumed to be rich in lipids to support the rapid growth of the pouch young in a thermally challenging environment. Lactating females require access to high-quality forage to maintain body condition while nursing successive offspring.

Maximum lifespan in this species has been recorded at approximately 13.2 years [am = approximately 13.2 years] for individuals maintained under captive conditions at 36.5 °C [T = 36.5 °C]. This longevity is notably high for a marsupial of such small body size, exceeding predictions based on allometric scaling relationships. Field-based estimates suggest that wild individuals rarely live beyond half this age due to predation, fire, and seasonal resource limitation. The maximum reproductive rate, expressed through a single joey per litter [N_R_i = a single joey per litter] with approximately one litter per year [F_R_i = approximately one litter per year] under ideal conditions, reflects a conservative life-history strategy where modest reproductive output is balanced by the relatively long reproductive lifespan afforded by the species' extended longevity.
